# An exponentially moving convex hinge and pointwise inverse-rate payment

This uses a new scale of tests inside the already established physical cone. The moving hinge produces upper-rate-tail inequalities with the reciprocal rate weight `1/r`; these do not follow merely by substituting a fixed convex nondecreasing rate function in the earlier log-perspective theorem. The geometric directional cap kernel then converts them into a payment at each positive inverse rate.

The proof uses the actual selected minima and their common separator. It is not asserted for arbitrary geometric defect sequences. It retains both open and closed rate tails, actual cap incidences, and the full original cap law. No lower bound on the captured term, and no OC numerical conclusion, is inferred.

## 1. Exact hypotheses and the new admissible field

Use the selected-minimum setting and the already audited full physical cone. On the current boundary normal bundle let

    Xi_j = W_j-beta_j+r_j+R_j,
    r_j=lambda_j(-log L_j)_+,
    lambda_j -> 0, beta_j -> beta,
    |R_j|<=C lambda_j.

The last expression is just the established decomposition: any difference caused by the positive part of `-log L_j` on `L_j>=1` is absorbed in the uniformly `O(lambda_j)` remainder, because the parameters have a common upper bound. The actual log measures and cap-load log measures have jointly retained limits

    (-log L_j)_+ eta_j delta_(r_j)
         -> ordinary_part_at_rate_zero + bhat,
    W_j(-log L_j)_+ eta_j delta_(r_j)
         -> ordinary_cap_part_at_rate_zero + ahat,
    0<=ahat<=bhat.

Their masses are bounded, `0<=W_j<=1`, and the exponential floor gives a common compact rate range with limiting defect rates in `[0,beta]`. The finite-PL representative `L_j=min_i A_ij` is defined on the common ambient space. It is positive on the current bodies; outside those bodies its values need not be positive.

Fix a threshold `R>0`, a nonnegative finite convex physical function `f`, and a continuous nonnegative normal weight `psi`. Define the actual physical field

    Phi_j(n,w) = psi(n) [f(w)-exp(R/lambda_j)L_j(w)]_+.          (1)

This field is globally finite, continuous, and convex in `w` for every fixed `n`: `-L_j` is a finite maximum of affine functions, so the expression inside the positive part is convex. Multiplication by the nonnegative normal scalar preserves this. No product of two physical convex functions has been used. The field is therefore an admissible test for the SAME exact separator at the current selected minimum, even though its coefficients grow exponentially with `j`.

Concretely, its actual body path is the audited normal-cut construction

    K_z^j(t)={X: n.X+t Phi_j(n,z,X)<=h_(K_z^j)(n) for every unit n}.

For each fixed `j`, this gives positive convex fibers for all sufficiently small `t>=0`, with signed inward first speed `Phi_j`. Convexity of the physical field preserves the Minkowski compatibility of all fibers, so their canonical hull has those exact sampled fibers and the same complete integer base. The permitted interval may shrink with `j`; local minimality supplies the separator on every one of these actual paths. No uniform finite step size is presumed.

On the current body, `0<=Phi_j<=psi f`. Let `F` be a uniform upper bound for `f` on the common compact support. The case `F=0` is trivial. Wherever the positive part is nonzero,

    L_j < F exp(-R/lambda_j),
    r_j >= R-lambda_j log F.                       (2)

Thus for all sufficiently large `j` its support has `r_j>=R/2`. On that support

    d eta_j/lambda_j
      = [(-log L_j)_+/r_j] d eta_j.                (3)

This exact relation supplies the needed bound after division by `lambda_j`; there is no assumption that arbitrary boundary area divided by `lambda_j` is bounded.

## 2. Passage at a continuity threshold

First take `R` for which the total defect measure gives zero mass to the rate slice `{r=R}`. Only countably many thresholds are excluded. Put

    p_j(w)=[f(w)-exp(R/lambda_j)L_j(w)]_+.

On the support in (2), `L_j=exp(-r_j/lambda_j)` exactly. Uniformly on compact rate sets strictly above `R`, `p_j` converges to `f`; uniformly on compact rate sets strictly below `R`, it is zero for large `j`. The functions are bounded by `F`. Their quotient by `r_j` is uniformly bounded by `2F/R`. Removing an arbitrarily small strip about the continuity threshold, then restoring it using the bounded limiting measure and Portmanteau, therefore passes these tests against both retained log measures.

Divide the exact separator inequality `int Xi_j Phi_j d eta_j<=0` by `lambda_j`. Equations (2)-(3) rewrite the main terms as

    int psi p_j/r_j d(ahat_j)
       -beta_j int psi p_j/r_j d(bhat_j)
       +int psi p_j d(bhat_j).

Here `ahat_j` and `bhat_j` mean the full current cap-load and unweighted log measures, before deleting their ordinary rate-zero parts. Those ordinary parts do not contribute because of (2). The remainder tends to zero: its absolute value is at most

    C int psi p_j d eta_j
       <= C lambda_j (2F/R) ||psi||_infinity
                       int (-log L_j)_+ d eta_j -> 0.          (4)

Passing the three main terms gives

    int_{r>R} psi(n) f(w)/r d ahat
       +int_{r>R} psi(n) f(w) d bhat
        <= beta int_{r>R} psi(n) f(w)/r d bhat.    (5)

The exact constant is unchanged. In particular no rate-dependent error survives the `1/lambda_j` rescaling.

## 3. Every open and closed positive-rate tail

For any `R>0`, choose continuity thresholds decreasing to `R`. The corresponding open tails increase to `{r>R}`. Since all integrands are bounded on rates at least `R`, monotone convergence of the positive terms proves (5) at that threshold as well.

Choose continuity thresholds increasing to `R`. Their open tails decrease to `{r>=R}`. Finiteness and the positive lower bound on the rate give

    int_{r>=R} psi f/r d ahat
       +int_{r>=R} psi f d bhat
        <= beta int_{r>=R} psi f/r d bhat.          (6)

Thus both endpoint conventions are proved, including positive rate atoms. Their difference is not automatically an inequality on the atom: subtracting two inequalities is invalid. At the top endpoint `R=beta>0`, however, (6) directly implies `ahat(rate=beta)=0` after testing `psi=f=1`, because the two unweighted surface terms coincide there.

The estimates make no assertion at rate zero, where `1/r` may be nonintegrable. The full kernel still retains that possible atom separately.

Adjoining the new condition makes the existing system strictly stronger: the new tails are not implied by the earlier convex-nondecreasing rate tests and the positive kernel. The tails alone say nothing about rate zero, so no unqualified equivalence or domination of the entire old system is asserted. For an exact algebraic check, put `beta=4/5` and, at one physical point and normal, set

    b=(1/6)delta_(1/5)+(1/3)delta_(2/5)+(1/2)delta_(3/5),
    a=(1/3)delta_(2/5).

Then `0<=a<=b`, and

    (beta-r)b-a=(1/10)[delta_(1/5)-2delta_(2/5)+delta_(3/5)].

Its pairing with every convex rate function is nonnegative by midpoint convexity. Thus all earlier nonnegative convex nondecreasing tests hold. But on an upper tail with `1/5<R<2/5`, its pairing with `1/r` is exactly `-1/3`, violating (5). The positive uniform kernel can also be applied to `b`, so merely adjoining that kernel does not repair the old implication. This is an exact separation of two systems of measure inequalities, not an assertion that these particular measures arise from an actual selected convex body or its cap law.

## 4. Directional canonical inverse-rate densities

Use the actual geometric normal-group cap theorem from `candidate e3baf104c92323ce`. Fix a nonzero oriented continuous gradient direction `e`. Keep the SAME full cap law `theta`. Its direction-`e` exterior and cap-load defects are `mu_e` and `alpha_e`, with

    alpha_e=int alpha_e,H dtheta(H),
    N_e=K mu_e,
    N_e,H=K(alpha_e,H+kappa_H s_e,H),
    kappa_H=e.u_H.

The section term vanishes unless `u_H` is parallel to `e`. The signed measure inside the cap kernel is not presumed positive for an outside exception. Actual `N_e,H` is positive. A continuous normal test equal to one at `-e` and zero at the other finitely many defect normals legitimately extracts this direction from (5)-(6); it does not select individual source labels or integer fibers.

For `R>0` define the canonical right-continuous physical-measure densities

    v_e(R) = int_{s>R} mu_e(dw,ds)/s,
    v_e,H(R) = int_{s>R} [alpha_e,H+kappa_H s_e,H](dw,ds)/s.     (7)

These are versions of the positive-rate densities of the actual inverse measures. The second formula starts as a signed tail, but it is a positive physical measure for every `R>0`, not just almost every `R`. To see this, it is a right-continuous finite signed measure-valued function locally in positive rate, agrees almost everywhere with the positive inverse density, and hence is a weak right limit of positive measures. The same argument applies after integration against the retained cap law. Joint compactification keeps every rate and section selection fixed.

Let `E_+(e)` be the records with `u_H` a positive multiple of `e`, and set

    v_e^noninside(R)=int_{H notin E_+(e)} v_e,H(R) dtheta(H).    (8)

For any record outside `E_+(e)`, its section term is zero or `kappa_H<0`. Hence, as physical measures,

    int_{s>R} alpha_e,H(dw,ds)/s >= v_e,H(R).

Inside records still have nonnegative boundary tail and may be dropped. Therefore

    int_{s>R} alpha_e(dw,ds)/s >= v_e^noninside(R).              (9)

All quantities in (7)-(9) are locally bounded in total mass at positive rates. In particular they may be tested by the prescribed physical convex `f`.

## 5. Payment at each individual positive inverse rate

Apply (5), isolate direction `e`, and use (9). Tonelli gives the exact physical-measure identity

    mu_e(dw,(R,infinity))
       = R v_e(R,dw)+int_R^infinity v_e(s,dw) ds.                (10)

Indeed each surface atom of rate `t>R` contributes `R/t+(t-R)/t=1`. Substitution proves, for every `R>0` and every nonnegative finite convex physical `f`,

    int f d v_e^noninside(R)
      + R int f d v_e(R)
      + int_R^infinity int f d v_e(s) ds
        <= beta int f d v_e(R).                                (11)

The upper integration limit can be replaced by `beta`. This is pointwise in the inverse rate, with canonical right limits. It is stronger than merely integrating a predetermined family of rate moments.

There is an exact closed-tail version. Define `v_e(R-)` and `v_e,H(R-)` by replacing `s>R` in (7) by `s>=R`; these are their finite left limits, and their noninside combination is again positive. Then (6) yields

    int f d v_e^noninside(R-)
      + R int f d v_e(R-)
      + int_R^infinity int f d v_e(s) ds
        <= beta int f d v_e(R-).                               (12)

The integral term is the same in (11) and (12): a single endpoint has zero Lebesgue measure. Thus every positive-rate boundary atom is accounted for without an unjustified disintegration of the old convex-rate test family.

When all direction-`e` surface defect is at one physical point and one rate `T>0`, its inverse density is constant on `(0,T)`. For any strictly capturing noninside cap collection of full-law weight `p`, (11) reduces to the previously obtained sharp incidence restriction `p+T<=beta`. With several surface rates, (11) instead controls the actual selected inverse density at each rate separately.

No universal lower bound on `v_e^noninside(R)` has yet been established. Such a lower bound must use actual deepestness, compatible fibers, and the full lattice structure; it cannot be supplied by deleting the inside section correction or by replacing cap incidences with closed-halfspace bits.

## 6. Exact localization to exposed physical zero faces

Let `A` be any affine function nonnegative on the limiting canonical body, and let `F={A=0}` within that body. For a nonnegative finite convex physical test `f`, define

    f_k=(f-k A)_+.

Each `f_k` is globally finite, nonnegative, and convex. On the common limiting support, `0<=f_k<=f`, and `f_k` decreases pointwise to `f 1_F`. Apply (5), (6), (11), or (12) with `f_k` and pass by dominated convergence. Every displayed inequality therefore remains true with all its physical measures restricted to the ENTIRE exposed face `F`, and with the original test `f` retained. The positive threshold keeps all inverse-rate factors bounded. The same argument applies to the earlier finite moment inequalities without inverse-rate factors.

Finite intersections of such zero faces are included by using the sum of their nonnegative affine functions. More generally, after a first face restriction the same argument can be repeated with an affine function nonnegative only on that face: domination is needed only on the already restricted measure's support. Thus successive exposed faces inherit the same inequality with the exact same `beta` and cap law.

This gives genuine physical-face conditioning, in addition to the proved normal conditioning. It does not select an arbitrary source row or integer fiber. In particular a source row's defect is supported on its affine zero face, but other source rows may have defect on the same face or its intersections. No subtraction of overlapping face inequalities is licensed.
